Mr. Chairman, what I wish to bring to the attention of the committee is not the need for something in the way of a building, but the need for greater care on the part of the department in the acquisition of properties. I intend to refer to a transaction which occurred right here in Ottawa in which it seems to me a price without warrant has been paid for a property acquired by the crown in comparatively recent times.
I go back to a situation which existed two or three years ago, when a firm in Ottawa known as Wittington Investments Limited acquired three properties on Isabella, Albert and Wellington streets from Norlite Realty Limited. The price paid for the three properties as shown by documents of record in the registry office was $967,500.
The Isabella street property was then sold by Wittington Investments Limited to an apparently related company, Wittington Realty and Construction Limited, under a deed dated May 1, 1954, and registered on July 22, 1954. The consideration for the sale of that property as shown by documents of record in the registry office was $204,268.61.
The second property on Albert street was also sold at that time, likewise to Wittington Realty and Construction Limited. The deed of the property was dated the same day, and it was registered on the same day as the deed for the Isabella street property. The consideration for the sale of that property as shown by documents of record in the registry office was $137,501.98.
We now arrive at the position where the third property, the Wellington street property, would be carried by Wittington Investments Limited at a net price of $625,730. The crown proceeded to acquire the property on .Wellington street. It served notice of expropriation, which notice was registered on March 26, 1954. Subsequently the compensation was arrived at, presumably by agreement, and conveyance was made and release given by the recipient of the compensation, namely Wittington Investments Limited. The consideration passing for this property as shown in documents of record in the registry office was $1,396,000. In other words, a property which had cost Wittington Investments Limited the net sum of $625,730 in 1952 was disposed of by that company to the crown in the fall of 1954 for $1,396,000. On the turnover Wittington Investments Limited realized an appreciation of capital or profit, whichever you like to call it, of $770,270 in a period of just two years.
On the face of it that kind of transaction calls for investigation and explanation. Here is a property which in the course of two years,

Supply-Public Works so far as the price paid by Wittington Investments Limited and the price realized by it on expropriation are concerned, has more than doubled in value. On the face of it there is something there that calls for investigation. Attention should be drawn to the fact that this was an expropriation, but apparently the compensation was determined by agreement.
I understand that in a case of that kind the practice of the department is to secure independent valuations from persons who are not only competent in their field but who can give sound advice and who should have no interest whatever in the transaction-I go further and say who should have no vestige of interest in the transaction.
I should like to know what independent valuations were obtained by the department which guided them in the paying of this enormous price, a price which I am informed on competent advice is not only grossly excessive but could not be defended under any circumstances. What were the valuations? What valuators supported this enormous price which was paid for this property by the crown?
My information-I trust that when the minister speaks he will give the committee full information-as far as it goes is that the appraisal was made by Mr. E. S. Sherwood.
I am told also that Mr. Sherwood is the manager of a building now in the course of construction by the same company, Wittington Investments Limited. I think the department will have to have some other source of independent advice to give any colour of justification to the payment of this exorbitant price for this property.
I am quite certain that the people of this country expect on the part of the government a sound businesslike approach to problems of this kind. When the crown finds it necessary to acquire property it should seek a property suitable for its purposes and by means which will guarantee the public as far as possible against being charged an exorbitant price. It is my understanding that the reason we have the procedure laid down in the Expropriation Act for the determination of compensation where the crown expropriates property is that the compensation to be paid shall be arrived at on proper grounds and after all relevant and proper testimony has been obtained.
This is not to exclude agreements where agreements can be entered into by the department in settlement of the compensation where it is obvious the department is obtaining a good price, thus saving the expense of litigation in the course of expropriation. But it is quite evident that was not the case here.


The mere fact that the price paid by the department for this property was double- yes, more than double-the cost of this property to the owner just two years before is enough, on the face of it, to condemn the price paid.
Far be it from me to introduce personal considerations, but the fact is that the gentleman who, I am told, conducted the legal affairs of the company which received this handsome premium on this investment was Mr. Duncan MacTavish, the president of the national Liberal federation of Canada. The fact that he holds that office is no disqualification of Mr. MacTavish-and I speak of a man who is, I am sure, a personal friend of many in this chamber-in carrying on his legal practice and acting for clients even in relations with the crown. But it was an additional reason on the part of the department for exercising the greatest care in a transaction of this kind that no suspicion should attach to it.
When we have, on the face of it, the fact that the price paid is double what the property cost the company just two years before, it seems to me that we have here patent facts which should have put the minister, or at least those of his officials who were in charge of this matter, on their guard and should have called for the exercise of much more vigilance in the public interest than has evidently been exercised in this case. If it were at an earlier stage of the session that we had learned of these matters, this is the sort of transaction that would call for inquiry before the public accounts committee.
At this stage of the session I raise the matter here on the estimates of the minister and say that even though the transaction appears now to be completed-evidently there is nothing, so far as I am aware, that can be undertaken now by way of undoing this transaction-nevertheless I put the house upon notice that the department, in negotiating with a company represented by the president of the national Liberal federation of Canada, has paid for this property, evidently willingly paid for it, more than twice the cost of the property to the owner just twc years before. I believe the house will wanl to know from the minister what were the independent valuations upon which the minister proceeded in paying a price that is on the face of it, palpably exorbitant.

Mr. Chairman, I shall only take about a minute. Last year when these estimates were before the committee I made a request that dredging, of which a gooc

deal takes place at the lakehead, be commenced earlier at Fort William. I should like to express appreciation because dredging started early in the spring, and that has helped employment very much in Fort William. I would repeat my request and ask that the dredging commence just as soon as possible. I know they have to have the report of the engineer on the sounding, but the dredging has to be done and I should like to see it commence as early in spring as possible.
I have nothing but commendation for the district engineers and their staff who are doing an outstanding job and co-operating thoroughly. As far as the minister himself is concerned, I have learned to have a great appreciation for the wise man who comes from the east. Since the time he first came here and swung his tennis racquet and walloped an outstanding tennis player of Canada, I have appreciated the work of the minister and that of his staff, and the courtesy of his deputy and engineers.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I cannot invite the minister to the opening of any public building in my constituency. But if some of the intimations I have received from him are justified, I can at least invite him to a fishing party when he completes the building of some wharves that I hope are forthcoming. We can sit on the end of the wharf and perhaps catch some tommy codfish.
I would suggest to him, however, that if we are going to keep that appointment and are starting from here, it will be advisable for him first to get the clocks fixed in this building. Otherwise, if he goes by one clock and I by another, one of us will get there too soon and the other too late. The clocks over the elevator entrances all show different times, and the chimes in the tower are erratic. Sometimes they strike the quarter hour at the half hour, the half hour on the quarter hour and the hour on either one. It reminds me of the ditty of the old Irishman's clock. How did it go? "When the hands are at nine the clock strikes seven and then I know it is a quarter to eleven." That is something the same as we have with the clocks at the moment. I hope the minister, with his engineering background and experience, will take care to see that at least when we do get out of here we shall get out on time. Otherwise we may not get out of here at all.
I did not rise to discuss the matter of keeping time. That seems relatively unimportant just now. I want to explore for a moment a matter of administration on which, frankly, I am not too clear in my own mind. I thought if it were not explored at this time rather than when the question is raised again,
Supply-Public Works
we might be told, "You should have done that when the estimates of the Department of Public Works were before you." The situation is that apparently somewhere between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport a fiasco of major dimensions has been created. We have the situation, according to the press, where the long awaited ferry which was constructed to ply between North Sydney and Port aux Basques now cannot use the harbour of Port aux Basques because of dredging there which has made the harbour too rough for use.
I know the Department of Transport does some dredging of its own. I remember that last year the Minister of Transport gave the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra quite a lecture when he suggested that his officers and engineers were more competent than those of any other department of government, and that they were the best qualified to do this work. It may be that the Department of Transport has done a great deal of this dredging. However, I notice in the report of the Department of Public Works that for the year ending 1954 dredging was done at Port aux Basques by contract. It refers to two areas in that harbour and gives the amount removed as over 6,800 yards drilled and blasted. In the year 1953 I find also in the report of the Department of Public Works that 15,225 yards were taken out of the harbour of Port aux Basques. I am not sure of the technical language, but it looks to me as though all of that had been drilled and blasted as well, but in that I might be mistaken.
It is apparent that during the years 1953 and 1954 the Department of Public Works has been doing extensive dredging in the harbour of Port aux Basques. Whether the Department of Transport was also carrying on dredging is something I do not know. I should hardly think it likely that both departments would be carrying on at the same time, but when you see the net result you would not be surprised at anything. You could not get a sillier situation than this government, between the various departments, spending on piers, dredging and ship construction an amount which according to the Halifax Chronicle-Herald is going to run to about $25 million, and when it is all done the ship has no place to go.
I know the Department of Public Works is not responsible for anything in connection with the ship, but what a ridiculous position some department is in. They built a ship for my constituency or one part of my constituency, to run from Yarmouth to Maine, and they forgot to put the engines in, so it could not run. In this case they built the ship

Supply-Public Works and put the engines in it, but now they have no place for the ship to go. It is a situation as to which I am sure the Minister of Public Works will give some explanation to this committee concerning the responsibility of his department.
In short, as I read it, what has happened is that the harbour of Port aux Basques in earlier days was protected by reefs and islands. In other words there were natural breakwaters there which gave the harbour substantial protection. But in preparing for this particular ship, the William Carson, to enter and leave that harbour freely, a great deal of blasting was done and a new channel was created; and in connection with that operation these natural reefs were blown out. Apparently no one ever thought that one of the functions of the reefs was to keep tidal waves from rolling in. Apparently someone was surprised. It was only a month or two ago they found out.
I notice that the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria put on the order paper early in May a question asking when this ship was going to start operations, and the Minister of Transport replied that no definite plan had been made in that regard at that moment. I can now easily understand why no definite plans were made at the moment; it was because they did not know where they were going to send it. In any event, they blasted out reefs; they blasted out islands, and now they find they cannot tie up the ship in the harbour. They built extremely expensive piers. There are side elevators. The three-inch clearance or three-inch rise and fall is all you can get against these elevators.
I am speaking now of something that is reported in the press. Now with the water surging back and forth in the harbour, it will rise far more than the three inches and therefore you cannot use the elevators. Therefore you cannot unload the ship. Therefore you have a painted ship not on a painted ocean but on an extremely rough ocean. The other day the Minister of Transport said, not in the house but in an interview to press men:
It Is proposed to carry out further work in the nature of a breakwater-
Having blown the breakwater out, you are now going to put it back, Mr. Chairman.
-in order to provide safer facilities for ships coming into the harbour-not only the William Carson, but all ships.
I would say in passing that I think all ships, including the one in which John Cabot -I almost said John Cabot Pickersgill- discovered Newfoundland, were able to lie in the harbour of Port aux Basques
(Mr. Nowlan.]

safely without experiencing rough water until these barriers were blown out. The Minister of Transport has been considering whether they are going to rebuild the reefs which apparently, as I take from the minister's look across the way, the department of the Minister of Public Works blew up, or whether they are going to spend another $1 million putting in artificial breakwaters.
In any event, as I said, I think the substantial part of this fiasco is perhaps with another department, but I at least want to know which department did it, so when the minister replies this afternoon I hope he will tell us. From a smile and a nod a few minutes ago I gathered that he would do so. I hope he will tell the committee whether his department did all this work, how long they have been doing it, how much they have spent in doing it, why they did it, and whether they did it on the instructions of the Department of Transport.
I notice that Mr. Baldwin, the deputy minister of transport, in his statement to the press says the Department of Transport must take the responsibility for this; but he also says that the technicians-whoever they may be-of the Department of Public Works were consulted and advised. It is a problem, as I said, on which we should have some more definite information than so far has been made available. How men and engineers who knew the sea and know something of those waters could play with firecrackers and blast these reefs and islands out in the way they did, without realizing what would happen afterwards, is something which I think is beyond the comprehension of most people. Certainly it is beyond the comprehension of the government member from the constituency of Burin-Burgeo who in an interview with the press, as reported in the Halifax Herald of Monday of this week, said he had been warning the government of this for five years.
He said:
A lot of Newfoundland seamen did too, but when we went to the C.N.R., they didn't seem worried because the government wasn't worried, and when we went to the government, the government wasn't worried because the C.N.R. wasn't worried. The project was not thought out well and I have my doubts whether what they have in mind now will be a remedy. It would be better to have two small boats rather than one big ship that is going to find it hard to get around the harbour, he said.
If there is any merit in the suggestion I know the Minister of Public Works, who is the minister from Nova Scotia, always wants to improve provincial facilities. I would suggest to him that he now take that big ferry which he cannot use and put it on the run

between Saint John and Digby so we can have a car ferry and bring the C.P.R. into Nova Scotia, or he can put it on the run from Digby to Saint John to Boston and we can enhance the passenger and tourist business and further to supplement the Yarmouth to Bar Harbor ferry. I think that would be better than to have this boat drop out of circulation for the two or three years it may take until they get this artificial breakwater built; and when they get that built it may not be any good anyway. However, that is the part of the matter which I wanted to explore delicately at the moment, and we shall listen with interest to the explanation by the minister later on.

I have listened with great interest to the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Digby-Annap-olis-Kings. It seems to me there is one obvious aspect of this matter of the harbour of Port aux Basques which he has overlooked, namely that the situation he has been describing may at least do something to help the unemployment situation.
I think perhaps this particular incident which I understand the minister is going to explain before this discussion concludes serves to lend colour to the suggestion that has come to my ears more than once, and it is this. While one cannot discredit the value of the technical knowledge of engineers there may be times when, in matters relating to the sea, more attention could be given to the viewpoints of those who are familiar with the various local conditions of tides, winds, waters and so on. I know I have had that suggestion made to me a number of times. It has been suggested that this aspect is sometimes overlooked by the engineers.
May I say that it was not said in such a manner as to suggest that the engineer does not perform a necessary function in our society. I know that when I passed through Port aux Basques last year I heard some remarks in current conversation about the situation that was developing in that harbour. Possibly I should have paid more serious attention to them than I was disposed to pay at that time. However, we may perhaps hear some further explanation of that subject.
The discussion on the first item of the estimates of the Minister of Public Works has become somewhat more extended and varied than appeared to be indicated when we started out. For my part I felt that last year we had quite a discussion on some of the policies which the then new Minister of Public Works was proposing to inaugurate. Some members, including myself, did indicate
Supply-Public Works
our general approval last year of the approach he then said he had in mind. My own feeling is that a period of one year is not sufficient time to be able to judge how far the minister is going to go in putting some of these policies into effect, one of which, as indicated by him, was that he was going to squeeze the water out of the public works estimates. I believe some progress has been made in that direction as far as the area of the country with which I am most familiar is concerned, and I hope that tendency will continue. I may have one or two suggestions to offer in that connection a little later in my remarks.
However, there is one item coming under the minister's department on which there was some discussion last year but which has not been referred to so far this year. I refer to the national highway building program which some of us think should be on a much more extended scale than has been undertaken so far. I note that in this year's estimates the major item for the trans-Canada highway is the same as in last year's estimates, which indicates that the scale of the national highway program is certainly not being extended.
During the past year I had the opportunity to do some travelling on some of our Canadian highways and some of the highways in the country to the south. I must say that by and large the comparison is not in favour of our Canadian highway system. It really does not seem to matter very much in what part of the country one travels; by and large that is the impression one gains. I travelled over a thousand miles on the highways of the province of Newfoundland last year, and from various quarters heard suggestions that they could very well do with an extended program of national highway development in connection with the trans-Canada highway. I think any member of the house who travels across that province will recognize, having regard to their population and their developed sources of wealth, that they are faced with a very difficult program with respect to extending across that province a highway which could properly be considered part of an adequate national highway system.
Following the Easter recess I returned across the continent by highway from Vancouver island to Ottawa, and I travelled most of the way on highways of the United States. It was my first trip by highway to eastern Canada, and I took what according to the map was the main highway route joining Canada's two largest cities. After having travelled several thousand miles on the highways of the country to the south of us, I must say it

Supply-Public Works
was a bit of a shock to discover what constituted the main highway between Canada's two largest cities. At the time the well known phrase, "nothing but an overgrown cow trail", seemed to describe it.
I also had the opportunity of doing a little travelling last year on some of the highways in our national parks. While I can see that quite a program is being carried on there, and I am glad to note that the appropriation has been increased in this year's estimates, nevertheless there is still a great deal of work to be done in western Canada before we can have even a single highway that can properly be called a transcontinental highway. I am not suggesting that I or any other member of this group would advocate going hog wild in the building of highways here, there and everywhere with assistance from the national treasury. I believe, however, that the highway program could and should be extended as part of the over-all transportation policy of the country.
If there is to be federal participation on an increasing scale, I believe that development must of necessity be correlated to a certain extent with the program of railway development that is to be undertaken. In developing our highway program all due consideration must be given to the existing railway structure of the country. I think some of the facts in relation to that matter became very apparent the other day in the meetings of the committee which was considering the bill having to do with agreed charges. I am not going to extend my remarks further on this point, except that I should like to know where I should send the bill for a tire ruined by a very bad pothole in a national park, whether to the Minister of Public Works or to his colleague the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. That was a very unexpected termination to a fairly good piece of road, and one of my front tires suffered as a consequence.
I should like very much to be able to take the minister and other members of the house on a little tour of some of the installations in Comox-Alberni that come under the harbours and rivers engineering division of the minister's department, but I am afraid if I were to follow the good example of the hon. member for Kootenay West my remarks would extend to at least a couple of hours. Therefore I shall not go into that matter very extensively. However, I should like to make one or two suggestions of a general nature. I referred earlier to the fact that last year the minister announced his intention of squeezing the water out of the estimates so we would know that when an item for a certain project appeared in the estimates,
fMr. Barnett.]
the department was seriously planning to undertake that particular construction in the ensuing year.
In line with that policy, I should like to suggest to the minister that a logical development would be the laying down of an overall plan with respect to the development of boat harbours, harbour protection works, wharves and floats for the coastal areas of British Columbia. We would then know with some certainty that when a certain project was undertaken it was a part of a logical over-all plan. It seems to me that would tend to improve the situation which so often arises now, when different local communities feel it essential to exert all the pressure they can command for the development of some particular project. If they knew that, generally speaking, a certain volume of projects could be undertaken by the department with the facilities available and with the money that could fairly be allocated for that purpose; if they knew there was going to be a logical development and that at the proper time the particular project with which they were most concerned would be proceeded with in due course, it seems to me that would enable not only the department but the people living in the area to have a much sounder approach to the matter of public works projects.
In that connection, and only because I feel it is a project which would fit in with the over-all development, I am going to mention what I consider to be the urgent need for the development of a more adequate small boat harbour at the important fishing centre of Alert Bay, which is on Johnstone strait just off the shore of Vancouver island proper. I know the people there were very hopeful that an item would be included in this year's estimates covering that project, and they are quite disappointed that such has not been the case. I would draw particularly to the attention of the minister at this time the desirability of that project as a part of the logical development of small boat harbours on the eastern coast of Vancouver island. There are others I shall not mention at this particular time.
There is one other matter with which I should like to deal which is connected with the same branch of the department. It has to do with the policy of the department with respect to the use and development of harbour facilities which are going to be required in increasing measure for automobile ferries. This is a matter which obviously involves the jurisdiction of both federal and provincial governments. I think the minister would agree the present situation has caused a good

deal of worry and uncertainty in the minds of many people on the coast of British Columbia.
Quite frankly, and I am saying this deliberately, I feel that some of the responsibility for this situation rests upon the shoulders of the public works department of British Columbia. So far as I have been able to observe their attitude has been rather erratic with regard to the planning they are undertaking in this direction. But I do feel I should suggest a change in federal governmental policy as it now stands on the basis of a letter I received from the minister last year. In this letter he suggested that because a certain harbour was going to be used primarily by a provincially-operated car ferry, the protective works necessary for that operation were not an urgent matter so far as the federal government was concerned. X refer specifically to the problem we had under discussion at that time, namely the ferry run between Hornby island and Denman island.
I feel that policy is not just what it should be. If the provincial government is prepared to subsidize the operation of a certain car ferry, presumably it is doing so only because it considers that particular service is of vital interest to the people of the communities involved. In other words it is not a matter of special facilities being made available for some few individuals. It is rather a general, community service. I feel that if we are to agree that automobile ferries are an extension of the highway system of a province, nevertheless when they involve the use of harbours which are in salt water areas and which have generally been accepted as the responsibility of the federal authorities, either under the Department of Public Works or the Department of Transport or a combination of both, it would be a logical arrangement if federal policy could facilitate the type of harbour protection needed rather because of, not in spite of, the fact the harbour facilities may be primarily used by a provincial ferry service.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that I was not going to attempt to carry you all around the many harbours and ports of the constituency of Comox-Alberni. Earlier in my remarks I did indicate that I had done some travelling to other parts of the country last year. I suppose because of that fact I have been asked to present to the house a certain petition, which I have pleasure in doing. When I have read it, I shall send it across to the Minister of Public Works, who undoubtedly is the custodian of such problems on behalf of members of this house. This is a petition to the 50433-353
Supply-Public Works
members of the House of Commons, Ottawa, and it reads as follows:
We the undersigned, Her Majesty's loyal subjects of Raleigh, in northern Newfoundland, do hereby petition the federal government of Canada for a public wharf in this community.
For the past five years we have requested such a wharf, but apparently our request has fallen on deaf ears, because no consideration has been given such a request.
Perhaps I might interject here that they may have appealed to me as a last resort, I do not know, but in any event I have been given the responsibility of presenting this petition. I shall go on and read the rest of it.
Raleigh is a fishing settlement in northern Newfoundland, and the only means of communication is by sea.
There is not a wharf in the community to which the coastal (C.N.R.) boat can dock. Transfer of sick from this area must be made by sea and provisions, etc., must come by sea. There are times when the sick, women and children cannot embark or disembark due to the heavy seas; yet no effort has been made to remedy this situation since confederation. The people of this area expected a better deal, and thought that improvements would be made where they were most deserving-but such has not been the case in Newfoundland since union. It is high time for an investigation into the building of public works in this province-they have not been placed in most places where they were most needed.
We humbly request that the federal government of Canada stop stalling and work in the best interest of the toiling masses of the dominion's youngest province.
We sincerely hope that this petition will be given the sympathetic consideration of Her Majesty's federal parliament.
It is signed by William Elliott and others. There are about two pages of names here. I am sure the Minister of Public Works will have great pleasure in taking this petition in charge, and I am sure that if he wants further details the member for that constituency will be pleased to provide them.
What is the constituency?
It is on the north shore of the province, in the constituency of the chairman of the marine and fisheries committee of this house.

committee that as long as item 353 is before us, I or the chairman will see any member who wishes to rise. The Minister of Public Works indicated that he wished to rise, and I see him.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I regret that I possibly will not be quite as complimentary as some hon. members who have spoken on this item. It is not because I do not admire the minister or his parliamentary assistant or those who are in the department. But certainly after the "slow boat to China" service we have for getting to the different floors of this building in this hot weather, we can quite appreciate that the expenditures on the elevators might well have been put on escalators so we could at least get to the floor we wish to reach a little more hastily than we do in the present circumstances.
I am pleased that the department has seen fit to call for tenders for the addition to the public building in New Westminster that they have been advertising for some time. I would point out to the minister, however, that it is not an unnatural thing for the citizens of a city the size of New Westminster to be unhappy about a fence, protective as it might be, on the main thoroughfare of their city for well over a year after the department began to tear down the building. After the building was torn down the fence remained facing the street for many months, and there is no possible sign of any further action being taken. I would point out to the minister and his officials that there is great danger of the road at what would be the back of the building caving in. I would urge that an examination of the area be made to make sure nothing dangerous happens and that no one gets hurt by a cave-in. The road is subject to quite heavy traffic. Possibly some means of support could be found to take care of the situation until such time as the building is begun and a new wall put in.
It is unfortunate that in deciding to erect this building provision was not made to house all of the various branches of the federal departments that are at present in the city of
[Mr. Winters.l
New Westminster. We have a condition today under which several federal government offices are spread throughout the city. Most of them will come into the new building. However, we are given to understand that the Department of Public Works office is to be transferred to the city of Vancouver. This, of course, makes the citizens of New Westminster quite unhappy, especially in view of a recent statement made by an august gentleman in the other house, Senator Tom Reid.
Usually I do not care to spend my time and the time of hon. members on a diatribe such as I am going to have to put on the record at this time. But I think it does call for some explanation from the minister, and certainly the people of New Westminster should know whether it is the attitude of the government, whether it is the attitude of the Minister of Public Works, or whether it is a new policy laid down by the Liberal party, which is different from that of the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier of whom we hear so much in this house. I am reading from the Vancouver Sun of Tuesday, April 12:
Senator Tom Reid said a funny thing the other day. He calmly announced to the New Westminster Liberal association that if New Westminster had elected Bill Mott, New Westminster would not have lost the federal public works office to Vancouver:	New Westminster, you see, elected a
Social Crediter.
What does Senator Reid mean-that the Liberal government in Ottawa took the office away from New Westminster to get even with the folks there because not enough of them voted Liberal to elect Mr. Mott?
You will see, Mr. Chairman, that charge is most serious. When people who know Senator Reid, as we have learned to know him in my area, as one who is straightforward and says what he thinks-and usually he thinks right in a thing like this-find him making charges that the Department of Public Works is discriminating quite deliberately against a city such as New Westminster because it did me the honour of sending me to this House of Commons as its representative, I think it requires some explanation and not just a shrug of the shoulders.
Further to that, the Vancouver Province apparently thought likewise, because on April 12 an editorial appeared in that paper to this effect. It is entitled:
Senator Reid Frowns on Politics
We were pleased to hear the other day that Senator Tom Reid frowns on governments-or politicians, we suppose-who play politics.
Speaking to a Liberal meeting in his home town of New Westminster, the senator criticized the Social Credit government's decision to double representation from Delta. Said the senator, sternly: "This is strictly a political move."
Having made himself clear on the subject of those who play politics, the senator proceeded to read a fatherly lecture to the assembled Liberals.

Strictly non-political, of course! Just a few words mourning the defeat of Liberal W. M. Mott at the last federal election.
And, said the senator regretfully, if Mr. Mott were still in parliament, New Westminster would not today be on the verge of losing the federal public works office to Vancouver.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a little time on this bill and ask hon. members to refer to the evidence which was presented to the Senate committee in connection with this case. For the benefit of those hon. members who have not the evidence before them I might say that the petitioner is a medical doctor. He alleged that his wife was suffering from drug addiction. On page 17 of the evidence he was being questioned regarding a visit to their home by his wife's father, who apparently also is a medical doctor. He was telling what happened at this particular time:
She was probably under the effect of drugs, and when she was lacking the drugs she was very nervous. I told her that her father and I decided to bring her to hospital. She said "I am in no state; I can't go." She was trembling. What I gave her was no narcotic; I gave her somnifeni, which was injected intravenously; that is like phenobarbital. I gave her an injection, and when her father came to my room I was giving it intravenously. As I say, that is not a narcotic; that is a drug people can have without a prescription.

Then we have the question by counsel:
Q. Is it correct that when Dr. Guibord, your wife's father, actually arrived at your domicile, you were at that very time injecting your wife?
A. I was not.
I should like to draw the committee's attention to the fact that in that paragraph he denied that he was injecting his wife, whereas in the previous paragraph he said that he was.
The question was "at that time".

He was asked:
Is it correct that when Dr. Guibord, your wife's father, actually arrived at your domicile, you were at that very time injecting your wife?
Previously he had said he was. The divorce is recommended on the evidence submitted by a young girl, aged 21. She apparently had stayed at the Ferron home for a year or more under welfare care. This was her foster home. This girl was being questioned:

A. Was I paid?
Q. Yes, were you paid by the welfare?
A. The welfare was paying.

A. A couple of times he did, until Mrs. Ferron accused us we were $10 missing and that it was either one of us had taken it and we would have to replace it by our allowance, and we never saw any more allowance after that.
Then this 21-year old girl is asked:

By Mr. Pager:

Q. Would you mind saying what kind of treatment-

Well, I will have to give testimony myself, I will have to say what I know, right away. She had a child.

The house in committee on Bill No. 492, for the relief of Georges-Etienne Cartier-Mr. Hunter-Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

I notice that in this bill one of the witnesses or investigators whose word is accepted is a man by the name of Maurice Pichette. In speaking on the other case I mentioned the growing contempt for the houses of parliament of Canada. This case shows it up maybe more than, or at any rate as much as, many another.
This investigator works for a firm known as the Reliable Detective Agency. I should like you to note the name "Reliable Detective Agency". The firm before that used to be known as the Fidelity Detective Agency. From the information I can gather it is very much the house of infidelity. The owner of this so-called reputable business institution is a man by the name of Gordon Etheridge. He does not only hire investigators; he also appears himself. In other words he is a working employer. He works right alongside of the many men he employs.
A year ago, in the parliamentary session of 1953-54, the employer, Mr. Etheridge himself, testified that he personally witnessed no less than 90 cases of adultery. How in the world the upper house can ever listen to a man 90 times over without beginning to ask questions is completely beyond my powers of comprehension, especially when a man testifies that he has to follow cases for weeks and sometimes for months on end, almost 24 hours a day, before he finally nabs them in the act of adultery. I am sure that in many cases he winds up on a dead-end street. Here he


shows up in 90 individual cases in which he says he was able to witness acts of adultery.
His employees, Mr. Chairman, are of no higher repute. This man Maurice Pichette who acted in this particular Cartier case was found guilty of having fabricated evidence before an Ontario court. He very haughtily says, however, that he was exonerated afterward. He was not exonerated, Mr. Chairman. The appeal court judge said in his concluding sentence; "however contemptible the conduct of the appellants may be considered . . ."; and he goes on to say in effect that he had to grant the appeal on a technicality. Yet even after all these things happen, the other place Is continuing to accept the word of this man under oath.
The same man was also found guilty and paid a fine of $200 in the province of Ontario for operating there without having obtained a licence. I hear there are a number of other things against him in the province of Quebec, but I have been unable to do the necessary research on that phase of the matter. However, I come back to my argument, and in conclusion I wish to emphasize to this committee the fact that the houses of parliament of Canada, in certain sections of Canada, are held in extremely low repute and that the opinion is growing, "Go to the parliament of Canada and you can get away with anything".

I should like to say something about this case after having read the evidence carefully. But in support of the argument my colleague has just made I think the committee might consider the credibility of the witnesses in this particular case. Might I remind the committee again of what my colleague has said, namely that one of the investigators, one Pichette, was convicted on the charge that he,
. . . with intent to mislead a court of justice, did unlawfully attempt to fabricate evidence by means other than perjury or subornation of perjury.
That is taken from the report of the case as set forth in the Ontario Weekly Notes No. 23 of June 17, 1955 and from which I read briefly as follows:
The facts of the case may be simply stated. The appellants, desiring to obtain evidence for the purpose of enabling a married woman to secure a divorce, planned to trap the husband into a false position from which adultery might be inferred or found if evidence was later given in some proceeding for divorce. This plan was to have a woman go to a room in an hotel, register under an assumed name, and give the room the appearance of the bed having been occupied. She was not required to do anything more. The husband was to be lured by a pretext to the room and, when there, could be found by the two appellants, who would then be in a position to give evidence as to his being found there with the woman. In carrying out this plan, the appellants arranged with

woman "A" to obtain the hotel room and perform her part of the plot, which she did. In the meantime, the appellants arranged with woman "B" to call the husband, under an assumed name, which was the name which woman "A" was to use at the hotel, and invite him to come to the room. This was done by woman "B", but the husband was suspicious. Woman "B" claimed to be a friend of the husband's sister, and the husband took the precaution of calling his sister as to the friend whose name he had been given over the telephone. Instead of going to the hotel room as invited the husband went to the police, with the result that the plan at that stage miscarried and it was the police who went to the hotel room, instead of the two appellants who were endeavouring to mislead someone.

The judge pointed out:
This ground of appeal, therefore, turns upon whether or not the Senate committee and parliament are a "court of justice" within the meaning of s. 177. In my opinion, they are not. The expression "court of justice", in the sense in which it is used in this statute, in my opinion, should be given the meaning attributed to the word "court" in Murray's English dictionary, vol. II, p. 1091, col. 1, under item 11, from which I quote the following:
"An assembly of judges or other persons legally appointed and acting as a tribunal to hear and determine any cause, civil, ecclesiastical, military, or naval."
In summing up the learned judge said:
In my opinion, therefore, however contemptible the conduct of the appellants may be considered, they have net been proved guilty of the offence charged, and effect must be given to the legal position taken by their counsel. The point which has been raised in the instant case, apparently for the first time, would appear now to be academic, because the legislation is entirely changed in the new Criminal Code, 1953-54, c. 51, which came into force on the 1st April, 1955.
These two men who were convicted appeared before the House of Commons special committee last night. I for one am unwilling on their evidence to convict Madame Cartier, who is named in this particular divorce case; and I invite members to read this evidence carefully. This bill, Mr. Speaker, has given me some concern over the past several months. I was approached on this matter last year, and at the time I last spoke in this house on January 13 or January 12 I appealed to the Prime Minister to relieve this house of the serious responsibility of dissolving marriages. Since that time we have waited in vain for the Prime Minister to tell the house what efforts, if any, were being made. The only conclusion to which we can come, in what we hope is the last month of the session, is that the Prime Minister is not making any effort to find a solution to this difficulty.
At the time I made the statement that I had been approached by members of the Roman Catholic clergy on behalf of certain cases, I said I would rather not name the clergy. One of the members of the house was indiscreet enough to take me up on that and rib me by saying that I did not name the clergy. In this case I do intend to name the clergy, and I have the permission of the clergy so to do. I should like to read into the record a letter I received dated March 7, 1955. I am prepared to file the letter, which reads in part:
The poor lady-
This is referring to the respondent, Mrs. Perras.
-has been notified that the Senate committee for divorces will hear her case on Friday, March 11. For the last three weeks, she had been on the verge of a nervous collapse.
Might I interrupt here, Mr. Speaker, to say that the usual procedure is for the husband to intimidate the woman for so many years until she finally agrees to sue him for divorce. He supplies the funds and she sues him for divorce. He does not contest the action, and everything appears to be aboveboard. In the process such low characters as were mentioned several minutes ago are employed and make a living. When you consider 90 cases

Private Bills-Divorce
at $300 each, I should like to call the attention of the Minister of National Revenue to the fact that I believe he has a real source of income tax available to him. However, I continue the letter.
The expectation was too much for her.
If I may again interrupt my reading of the letter, Mr. Speaker, yesterday down in room 118 when we had a meeting of the committee, the lawyer for the petitioner asked the woman who was attempting to defend her case, "Madam, why are you defending this case"? Naturally, the woman broke down, as any decent, self-respecting woman would.
I should like to challenge any member of this House of Commons to ask his wife, "Madam, why would you like to save your marriage?" I continue the letter.

She committed adultery,
admittedly.

The hon. member who is now interrupting does enough interrupting in the committee meetings.
February the 26th, she tell sick and the doctor had to be called. She was sent to hospital and since then has been in bed under treatment. She had a blood transfusion-
They do not give blood transfusions, Mr. Speaker, for the fun of it.
-daily serum and was seen by the hospital's psychiatrist.
Now, she will not be able to go to Ottawa this Friday. The lawyer asked for a written statement from her doctor and is going to present the committee with that letter. The doctor is even ready to go to Ottawa and testify if necessary.
What I am afraid of is that the adverse party tries to pull a fast one on her and win the case by default.
I simply think that it is criminal, even for a husband to frighten and torture his wife so much in order to get his goal that she totally collapses under the strain and tension. Such ignominious behaviour should be punished and I am really deeply shocked by the fact that our laws permit such events to happen.
I trust you to be able to stop a divorce that could be obtained under such circumstances. If you feel it may be useful to use my name and letters in that case, don't hesitate to do so.
May I thank you again for the care you took of that case.
I am very truly yours,
Capt. Rev. Robert M. Rivest, Headquarters Quebec Command, 3530 Atwater Avenue,
Montreal.
He is the Roman Catholic army chaplain there. This is a case in which, if the mover of the bill insists, we intend to call for a division of this house. I do not know whether or not Mrs. Perras has ever committed adultery. I intend to be quite honest. She claims in her evidence before the other place that she is not guilty of committing adultery. Others claim she has, amongst whom are
the employees of this famous Mr. Etheridge, of Montreal, and his Reliable Detective Agency, especially a certain Mr. Maurice Pichette, who has been convicted of fabricating evidence. However, even granting that this woman may have committed an error,
I think in this case we should pursue the policy that was pursued yesterday down in the committee.
Now, Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the committee we had the case of an honest woman. She came to the committee and attempted to preserve her marriage, and honestly admitted that she had been guilty of committing adultery. I am very pleased that by an overwhelming vote the committee decided not to grant her husband's suit for divorce. The consensus, if I gauged it rightly, was that even though this woman had committed a wrong, she had done so after extreme provocation, running over a number of years, on the part of her husband, and therefore if anybody was deserving of a decree of divorce it was the woman and not the man. However, the committee's hands were tied. We had to vote either for or against the man's petition, and we decided by an overwhelming vote that the case was unworthy of further attention in this house.
My reason for not even wanting to let the Perras case go before the committee on miscellaneous private bills is that this case is built on the testimony of men who have shown their contempt for the houses of parliament of Canada. I believe the case a worthy one even on its own merits. However, if this parliament wants to maintain its dignity, it has to show some action.
I have repeatedly appealed to the Minister of Justice on this issue. He has hedged ever since we began to appeal to him a year ago. I asked a year ago, who is responsible for maintaining the dignity of the houses of parliament when testimony is given before them under oath? The minister, after some shillyshallying, finally came forward with the answer that it was the attorney general of the province of Ontario. Now a year later, when the attorney general of the province of Ontario has taken action and has been able to obtain a conviction, it is found by the Ontario court of appeal, and on a technicality, that those people cannot be adequately dealt with. The minister says the new section of the new Criminal Code is designed to look after these people. However, the minister has not yet satisfied this house and the country-
